REI’s take on the Alpha hoody is soft, warm, and has a better layering fit than others we’ve tested. Plus, it’s cheaper than most other hoodies on the market thanks to REI’s house-brand price modeling.

Recent findings suggest that crocs might rule the camp shoe world, but we’ve been loving this alternative from a small, Columbia-based manufacturer that uses sustainably-sourced materials, hires a mostly local workforce, and donates money to nonprofit spay/neuter programs. Not to mention, the shoes themselves are pretty great: they pack down flat for backpackers to wear in town or at camp, and they make a supremely comfortable recovery shoe.

According to recent reports, inspiration from the couch might be the final push someone needs to take the plunge and commit to their next trip. This coffee-table-worthy book covers 50 of the best hiking trails in North, Central, and South America, ranging from six months on the Pacific Crest Trail to overnight treks in Peru. Each trail profile was written by someone who actually hiked it and includes logistical information such as seasonality, gear lists, and transportation.

It’s hard to dethrone the NeoAir XLite, which continues to offer an impressive combination of weight, packed size, and warmth—there’s a reason it’s one of the most popular inflatable sleeping pads on backpacking trails. Win-win.

A good sun hoodie is an integral part of sunny or warm-weather hikes. Free Fly’s recently upgraded blend of bamboo fibers and polyester is more durable and pill-resistant than previous versions, without losing the brand’s signature softness. This also makes a great travel shirt, and the slightly oversized fit provides non-clingy coverage without feeling baggy and sloppy, so you can go for your hiker’s standard size.

Keep your favorite backpacker cozy (and less stinky) with this base layer shirt that combines merino and alpaca for extra softness and odor resistance. This versatile top can pull triple duty as a camp shirt for sleeping, a cold-weather base layer for hiking, or even a ski shirt for days at the resort. This top has excellent articulation through the shoulders, fits well under an outer layer, and has flat-stitched seams that don’t chafe under pack straps. For another alpaca option with a higher percentage of alpaca wool, we love Alpacas of Montana’s quarter-zip, which has a long hemline that doesn’t shift around under a backpack hip belt.

This is a gift for your own peace of mind and your favorite hiker’s safety. The inReach Mini 3 Plus has all the usual features of a typical Garmin messenger, like GPS live tracking, text messaging, and a one-touch SOS button. But the Mini 3 Plus also adds voice memos, photo sending, and larger message capacity to its toolkit. If you really love your giftee, you can cover their subscription, too.

These days, most hikers and backpackers take at least one rechargeable device on their trips, whether it’s a smartphone, Bluetooth headphones, or a rechargeable headlamp. Anker’s fast-charging and impressive weight-to-power ratios got even better this year with the 20,000mAh Zolo Power Bank, which can charge a modern smartphone around four times and juice up to 50 percent capacity in just over 30 minutes. This battery pack is a good size for longer trips, but you can also grab the 10,000mAh version, which weighs just over eight ounces and is optimal for shorter trips with less time between town stops.

In a recent development, unless your recipient is heading for a specific thru-hike—in which case FarOut’s individual trail downloads are a safe bet—Gaia has some of the most user-friendly interfaces and simplest download procedures among offline mapping apps. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

It has been revealed that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing substantial things.”.

Actually, major is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a upcoming best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

It has been revealed that there’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

It has been revealed that “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a massive challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Recent findings suggest that finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

Sources indicate that she also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

According to recent reports, the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

According to recent reports, “I just set it and left it,” she remarked. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

It has been revealed that “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she noted. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

Recent findings suggest that “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

In a recent development, working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

In a recent development, “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she noted of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Recent findings suggest that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

Sources indicate that “There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

Sources indicate that as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case stated. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

Industry News: Grand Theft Auto 6 Is Here. Goodbye, Winter Training Plan.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on my run this morning, the streets of Upcoming York seemed a little emptier.
  • Across the country, a lot of people have come down with a sudden and very specific illness.
  • In a recent development, here’s the thing, though: for a game about crime, a surprising amount of it is about nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on my run this morning, the streets of Upcoming York seemed a little emptier. You may have noticed the same thing in your part of the world. It is not the Rapture. It’s Grand Theft Auto.

Across the country, a lot of people have come down with a sudden and very specific illness. Even the man who profits from it saw this coming. Back in April, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said, “I think a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19.” One economist puts the cost in lost productivity at around $1 billion. To be fair, it’s been a long wait. GTA V came out 13 years ago. My daughter was in daycare then. (That was the only time I could sneak in some game time.) She is now a freshman in high school.

In a recent development, here’s the thing, though: for a game about crime, a surprising amount of it is about nature. I mean, there’s a National Park you can explore. It’s been less than 24 hours, and my Instagram feed has already served up players feeding NPCs (the game’s random bystanders) to alligators and a Bigfoot lurking near a swamp called Cottonmouth Lake. The Bigfoot is the Skunk Ape of actual Florida folklore. It knocks you out with noxious fumes, and the last thing you see is a pair of giant hairy feet coming toward you. In its demented way, it’s a Florida nature documentary. Which is to say: you are about to lose a lot of people to the swamp.

Then there’s the time commitment. Rockstar Games states one of its studio heads needed about 80 hours to get through the story, side quests included. That’s a 16-week marathon build at five hours a week. For those of us with a training plan to execute, a ski trip on the calendar, and a whole winter we’d actually like to spend outside, the math is cruel. Like me, you may be suffering from GTA FOMO.

In a recent development, when GTA IV came out in 2008, it was easily the best game I’d ever played. It was set in Liberty City, a barely disguised New York City. Niko Bellic, the main character of the game, had a story that was darker and more grown-up than anything the series had tried before: a war-haunted immigrant chasing the American dream through its back alleys, with the pathos of a Michael Mann criminal. Plus it was fun to just walk the streets. That spring I interviewed Dan Houser, one of the game’s creators, for GQ. I asked him why New York was the perfect setting. “You just meet freaks everywhere,” he told me. He described a guy who walks up with a CD player and asks if you like hip-hop, “the real stuff.” Say yes, and it turns into a little scene with people laughing at you. “We were inspired by living here.”.

It has been revealed that this latest GTA received the same obsessive treatment, this time in Florida. Rockstar has had a research team based in Miami for years, and its developers have described riding along with ex-cops, hitting the clubs, and logging beach time, all so that Leonida, the game’s version of Florida, would feel like a real place.

I never finished GTA V. Its release coincided with newly introduced fatherhood and a new gig, and, well, I chose to be a responsible adult. I’m told this was the right call. My character is presumably still sitting in a stolen car somewhere outside SoCal inspired Los Santos, engine running, waiting for me. To be honest, I didn’t love it the way I loved IV anyway. But VI, if all the reviews are correct, is a masterpiece. My kids now know how to operate the microwave. So I will be playing it.

Meanwhile, the real outdoors isn’t going anywhere, and neither is my list: I’ll be hiking in Mexico next week, off-roading in Texas in December, and maybe squeezing in a ski trip. But there is GTA that must be played. I believe in you. You can do both. Run in the morning, steal cars at night. Don’t neglect your children or your pets if you have them. But if you miss a few runs, fine. Maybe that spring race isn’t the one where you go for the PR, you know?

Sources indicate that so take some comfort: as you hunker down this winter, you are still communing with nature, technically. Just watch out for the alligators.

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh).

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-newly introduced TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

According to recent reports, the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#9536. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1515 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm.
  • Industry observers note that but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important.
  • But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

Industry observers note that but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin indicates.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

According to recent reports, scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s crucial to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

According to recent reports, before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

Loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin notes. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney claims. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

In a recent development, when descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

It has been revealed that with your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

Keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

In a recent development, you might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin claims. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”.

In a recent development, it comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

Sources indicate that rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

Sources indicate that and before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney says. “You can just sort of ride it.”.

Sources indicate that on a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

Recent findings suggest that when surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

According to recent reports, on particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

Sources indicate that “I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin notes. “I never feel like I have that much control.”.

Martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

In a recent development, if you’re shouldering a particularly significant pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

It has been revealed that but if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28.
  • There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running.
  • One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and will be updated with additional sources shortly.

There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

Sources indicate that for the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:.

Race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Recent findings suggest that two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI revealed the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”.

Beyond UTMB officials, stakeholders in this decision included the towns up and down the Chamonix Valley and the regional government. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

The 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

Industry observers note that from the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti notes. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”.

But coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

In a recent development, UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour company Run the Alps.

The only question is which one fits the person you’re shopping for.

In a recent development, for the person who values versatility but travels light, the Skeletool CX is an everyday-carry upgrade they’ll actually use. Think travelers, hikers, cyclists, and anyone who likes being prepared without dedicating half a pocket to a tool. At just five ounces, it combines a knife, pliers, wire cutters, bit driver, and bottle opener in one streamlined package, striking an impressive balance between capability and portability. The customizable bit driver even stores an extra bit in the handle, making quick gear adjustments easy when you’re on the move. Available in a range of colors and customizable options, it’s a practical gift that feels personal, too.

Sources indicate that not everyone needs a multitool. Some people can get by with a really good knife. The Skeletool KB delivers exactly that, pairing a lightweight folding blade with a bottle opener built into the pocket clip. Weighing only 1.3 ounces, it’s a thoughtful upgrade for the person who always likes to have a knife within reach. The one everyone turns to when a box needs opening, a tag needs cutting, or ribbons need snipping off a holiday gift. Practical, affordable, and available in a range of colors, the Skeletool KB proves that sometimes the simplest gifts get the most use.

The Skeletool KBX takes the simplicity of the KB and adds a little grit. Its combo blade pairs a straight edge with a serrated section, making it a natural fit for people who put their gear to work. It’s the kind of knife that is just as likely to live in a tackle box or hunting pack as it is in a pocket. Durable and customizable, it’s a thoughtful gift for someone who believes good gear should be used, not babied.

Recent findings suggest that some people can’t help themselves. Give them a loose hinge, a wobbly chair, or any project that needs finishing, and they’ll start looking for a tool. The Rebar was built for exactly that kind of person. One of Leatherman’s longtime bestsellers, it packs 17 tools into a compact design, including pliers, wire cutters, screwdrivers, a file, a saw, and both straight and serrated blades. Whether they’re restoring an old piece of furniture, tying custom flies, or bringing a long-neglected project across the finish line, the Rebar is ready to help. Give the Rebar to the person who would rather figure it out themselves than wait for someone else to do it.

Some people have a reputation for being prepared. Get that person on your list the Wave Plus. Considered one of Leatherman’s most iconic multitools, the Wave Plus packs 18 tools into a durable, easy-to-carry design. What sets it apart is accessibility: many of its most-used tools can be opened with one hand and accessed without unfolding the entire tool, making quick adjustments and repairs that much easier. More capable than a pocket knife but compact enough to carry regularly, it’s the multitool for people who like having an answer ready before the question is even asked. And like all Leatherman tools, it’s backed by a 25-year warranty.

Sources indicate that founded in 1983 by Tim Leatherman, Oregon-based Leatherman Tool Group is the world’s largest manufacturer of high-quality multipurpose products with distribution in more than 86 countries. Built upon three principles, unwavering perseverance, ingenious design, and the ability to save the day, Leatherman has empowered people around the world to solve problems, major and small. #9533. Industry News: Gary Colliver Was a “Substantial-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

Industry News: Gary Colliver Was a “Substantial-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

Recent findings suggest that to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions noted. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Sources indicate that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management proposal for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

According to recent reports, “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial blueprint was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

As a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular significant wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

#9531. Breaking: A Hiker Fell off a Cliff in Major Bend National Park. Then Rescuers Had to Leave Him There Overnight.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (478 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A Hiker Fell off a Cliff in Major Bend National Park. Then Rescuers Had to Leave Him There Overnight.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard).
  • A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Substantial Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard).

A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Substantial Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.

Recent findings suggest that according to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction.

The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission.

Sources indicate that “The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, noted in a statement. “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.”.

Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground.

It has been revealed that just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission debuted with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was uninjured, and secured him in a rescue vest to lift him into the aircraft. The mission was finished by 10:45 A.M., and the hiker was transferred to Big Bend Regional Medical Center.

“During a complex hoist operation in rugged, inaccessible terrain, our medevac crew successfully reached and evacuated an injured hiker when no ground rescue option existed, delivering the patient safely to higher medical care,” Lt. Col. Teresa Parrotta, commander of the 29th Combat Aviation Brigade, Maryland Army National Guard, said in a statement.

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Major Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city. It’s rugged, isolated, and enormous, spanning 800,000 acres with sheer 1,500-foot limestone cliffs. The National Park Service warns visitors to expect unreliable cell service, sparse infrastructure, and primitive roads—conditions compounded by the intense Chihuahuan Desert sandwiched between the Chisos Mountains. Reaching a hiking trailhead is challenging because roads frequently wash out from flash flooding, and many backcountry trails require high-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

#9530. Breaking: Connor Herson Explains How He Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Freerider’ in Just 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2352 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Connor Herson Explains How He Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Freerider’ in Just 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connor Herson enters the Monster Offwidth on 'Freerider' after sending 'The Prophet' earlier that day.
  • It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connor Herson enters the Monster Offwidth on 'Freerider' after sending 'The Prophet' earlier that day. (Photo: Courtesy of Tommy Caldwell).

It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me. I don’t do dangerous stuff.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. I had my own project on Leaning Tower, and it was taking all my time this season.

In a recent development, on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Recent findings suggest that packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and promptly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

According to recent reports, I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

Sources indicate that the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

Sources indicate that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

According to recent reports, within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex, “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!”.

Industry observers note that alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Freerider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Freerider this afternoon if you want!”.

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Sources indicate that among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

Industry observers note that the climbing on Freerider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Freerider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Sources indicate that around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Freerider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

Industry observers note that at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Freerider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we swiftly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Freerider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

In a recent development, nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

#9524. What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1238 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).
  • Recent findings suggest that on the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected.
  • Sources indicate that that’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).

Recent findings suggest that on the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected. The terrain was brutal, with steep descents over sharp, rocky granite tracks along the 6,345-foot Jebel Jais summit. My heavy pack weighed me down, and I could feel every stone beneath my boots. By day three, my two massive toes hurt so much that on one challenging descent, I collapsed and couldn’t take another step.

Sources indicate that that’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me. He saw that I was struggling and stopped to pull out a roll of tape from his bag. Then, he peeled off my very stinky hiking socks without a second thought, taped up my toes, and bandaged my knees. He even carried my pack for several miles, guiding me down the remaining steep sections.

This stranger had no reason to go out of his way to help me, and I know I could not have finished that day without him. Hikers call this kind of experience “trail magic.” The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines the term as any instance of finding what you need most when you least expect it; experiencing something rare, extraordinary, or inspiring in nature, or encountering unexpected acts of generosity that restore one’s faith in humanity.

Recent findings suggest that trail magic is often associated with Appalachian Trail history from the early 1980s. However, after my experience in the UAE, I started wondering what it looks like elsewhere. So, here are five stories from other hikers who have experienced trail magic in one form or another around the world.

Recent findings suggest that matt Jordan, a hiking and backpacking guide with Intrepid Travel, was walking Newly introduced Zealand’s 1,881-mile Te Araroa Trail southbound in 2023 when he hit the muddy Longwood Forest in Fiordland. After a miserable day of rain and bog, he pushed on toward Turnbull’s Hut, one of the last backcountry huts on that segment. He’d heard that sometimes, free supplies were stored there for hikers passing through. As he approached, he prayed it hadn’t already all been taken by the time he got there.

In a recent development, “Thankfully it hadn’t,” he indicates. When he opened the store area, he found a cache of goodies.

“A local man who hikes in supplies, hauls out trash, and maintains the hut about twice a month leaves coolers stocked with beer, soda, and candy bars,” Jordan says. Excitedly, he grabbed a drink, then promptly slipped in the mud and fell on his backside. After days of awful weather conditions, though, that didn’t stop him from laughing out loud.

Sources indicate that “For me, the gesture was about more than a cold drink. It was a reminder of the generosity of strangers and the sense of community that makes long-distance hikes unforgettable worldwide.”.

Meeta Singh Rao, a hiking guide in India, notes some of her best trail magic came from shepherds who spend months in the high mountain pastures of the Indian Himalayas. In October 2022, she was leading a trek to Nawali Bugyal in Uttarakhand when the weather turned. Heavy rain began to fall, and strong winds blew. The mules carrying their gear were also lost, and camp was miles away.

In a recent development, the group came across a shepherd with his flock. He heard where they were headed, and offered them shelter in his channi, a mountain hut made of stone, mud, and plastic sheets. “When rainwater leaked through the roof, he walked out into the downpour to rearrange the plastic so we stayed dry,” notes Rao.

Recent findings suggest that when Rao offered to pay, the shepherd gently refused, saying they were his guests. “A couple with so little of their own opened their home to us, giving us a feeling of belonging in the mountains,” she adds.

Industry observers note that kaitlyn Bussell has walked four Caminos. But her second, the 62-mile Camino Inglés in September 2023 through Galicia, was particularly challenging. The rain was constant, few hostels and cafés were open in the fall, and she walked long stretches without seeing another pilgrim.

On the second day, wet and ready for a break, she ducked into the first bar she found for a café con leche and to charge her phone. When she went to pay, the young woman behind the counter told her the coffee was free and handed her some water, prayer cards and a small Camino keepsake.

According to recent reports, “It was a small thing, but it came at exactly the right moment,” Bussell recalls. “After days of rain, it lifted my spirits and made me realize that this pilgrimage is as much about the people you meet as it is the miles you walk.”.

Industry observers note that on Japan’s Shikoku 88 Temples Pilgrimage route, Lauren Roerick and her brother were leaving one of the temples when she spotted a sign offering matcha tea ceremonies for pilgrims. They initially walked away unsure whether they would be intruding but returned and decided to try it anyway.

According to recent reports, “A Japanese man welcomed us inside where two women in kimonos were preparing and serving matcha under his instruction,” adds Roerick. “To make us feel welcome, he called a friend and had her on speakerphone, translating the whole ceremony from Japanese into English.” Lauren and her brother learned about the tradition, tried making tea themselves, and ate small Japanese sweets.

“It was proof that trail magic isn’t always a bottle of water or a helping hand,” notes Roerick. “Sometimes a stranger opens his door, works around a language barrier, and shares a bit of culture with people passing through.”.

Recent findings suggest that on a windy hike to Matterhorn Base Camp, Libera Pagano, tour director with EF Adventures, noticed an older woman struggling. The altitude made her dizzy, her legs were shaking, and her friend had walked far ahead. “I offered to sit with the woman while she rested behind a large rock and we started chatting,” says Pagano.

That’s when Pagano learned it was the woman’s 86th birthday, and the hike was a present she’d given herself. They stayed together, and when the woman felt ready, they walked slowly until they caught up with her companion. When the group met back at basecamp, the woman told Pagano that without her help, she would never have made it to the summit.

Industry observers note that “I thought nothing of what I had done,” says Pagano. “But for that woman, it was the difference between giving up and fulfilling her birthday wish.”.

In a recent development, I never learned the name of the man who bandaged my toes in the Hajar Mountains, and I probably never will. But I think about him whenever I struggle on a trail or see another hiker limping.

All these stories have one thing in common—human compassion. Sometimes that is stopping to help a stranger in need, sharing what little you have, or leaving a cache of supplies for a hiker you’ll probably never meet. These gestures don’t have to be grand or cost much, but they can make an enormous difference and are an easy thing to pay forward so everyone experiences a little magic outdoors.

#9520. Industry News: How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1376 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The author's girlfriend, Lucy Drury, after the sun set on 'Diedre.' (Photo: Audrey Callaway).
  • According to recent reports, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Newly introduced York near the Gunks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author's girlfriend, Lucy Drury, after the sun set on 'Diedre.' (Photo: Audrey Callaway).

According to recent reports, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good firm.”.

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Newly introduced York near the Gunks. Presently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her substantial three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

According to recent reports, callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

According to recent reports, I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

Industry observers note that when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

Industry observers note that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we promptly got all our stuff together.

It has been revealed that we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

Recent findings suggest that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

It has been revealed that very swiftly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

We got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Sources indicate that then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

Recent findings suggest that so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Sources indicate that every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

It has been revealed that at one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he noted it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never highlighted it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

Industry observers note that we got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

It has been revealed that I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a substantial light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

In a recent development, to really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Fresh York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

Industry observers note that as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.
